questions.prompt: Why is Event ID 4624 nearly meaningless without its Logon Type field?
options: 4624 is only logged on domain controllers
The Logon Type determines what actually happened -- Type 3 (network share access) is routine, while Type 10 is RDP and Type 9 is a strong lateral movement signal
The Logon Type contains the source IP address
questions.explanation: Treating all successful logons alike either buries real findings in share-access noise or overstates routine activity as intrusion.

questions.prompt: Why is Event ID 4688 close to useless without additional configuration?
options: It is disabled on all modern Windows versions
Recording the command line is a separate policy setting -- without it you get an image path and no arguments at all
It only logs processes that failed to start
questions.explanation: Without 'Include command line in process creation events' enabled, there is no visibility into encoded commands, script paths, or targets -- which is most of what matters.

questions.prompt: Why does Event ID 1102 survive the action it describes?
options: It is stored in a separate protected log
It is written after the clear operation completes, so the record of the clearing remains in the newly-empty log
It is replicated to all domain controllers
It cannot be cleared by administrators
questions.explanation: Clearing the Security log destroys its prior contents but generates 1102 immediately afterward -- making it one of the highest-signal events available.

questions.prompt: What does Event ID 4648 indicate, and why does it matter on a workstation?
options: A logon using explicitly supplied credentials rather than the current token -- unusual on a workstation, and it names both source and target accounts
questions.explanation: Explicit credential use is how stolen credentials get applied to remote systems, so a 4648 naming a privileged target from an ordinary workstation warrants investigation.
